title: Athens: listen, locate, question
reviewStatus: AI-assisted research draft · human editorial review pending
geometryNotice: Illustrative layout, not to scale. The court, columns, paths and rocky rise are original schematic geometry, not surveyed remains or a reconstruction of Paul's exact route. No invented dialogue is included.

periods.label: Roman-period setting · Acts 17
periods.note: Follow the order of Acts 17:16–34. This pilot does not assign an exact year, duration or walking route to Paul's visit.

periods.label: Modern archaeological record
periods.note: Read the same places through excavation and conservation evidence. ASCSA began its Agora excavation in 1931; the Greek Ministry documents site-presentation works in 1997–2004. These later records do not independently verify every event narrated in Acts.

sources.title: USCCB · Acts 17, especially the note on 17:19
Greek Ministry of Culture · Ancient Agora and Areopagus presentation works

stops.title: A visitor in Athens
stops.textNote: Acts places Paul in Athens while he waits for his companions. Read the verse's own account of his response to the city.
stops.evidenceNote: The Agora excavation project describes a civic setting that combined commercial, political and legal activity. That city context is broader than one episode in Acts.
stops.uncertainty: Acts 17:16 supplies no street address or route for this waiting scene. The opening marker is a reading aid, not a recovered location.

perspectives.paul: Which response does the narrator attribute to Paul in verse 16? What does the verse leave unsaid?
perspectives.listener: Before the conversations begin, whose view of the city has the narrator given you?
perspectives.archaeologist: What kind of evidence could identify a city setting, and what would be needed to identify one person's movements?

stops.title: Conversations in the marketplace
stops.textNote: Acts describes discussions in the synagogue and marketplace, then encounters with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. The scene below illustrates a public gathering space only.
stops.evidenceNote: ASCSA reports inscribed public documents, standards for weights and measures, and jurors' tickets and ballots among Agora finds. These objects support civic and administrative activity; they do not record this conversation.
stops.uncertainty: The pilot does not identify a synagogue building, stall, philosopher's school or precise point at which Paul spoke.

perspectives.paul: Which different audiences does verse 17 distinguish? What topic does verse 18 attribute to Paul's teaching?
perspectives.listener: Compare the different reactions recorded in verse 18. Does the text make all listeners agree?
perspectives.archaeologist: How do weights, legal records and ballots help describe a public space without establishing the words spoken there?

stops.title: What does Areopagus identify?
stops.textNote: The narrative moves to the Areopagus and records a request to hear the teaching explained. Keep the name in view while checking the translation and its notes.
stops.evidenceNote: The USCCB note on Acts 17:19 identifies two possible senses: the hill of Ares or the Athenian council. This interpretive uncertainty prevents a confident pin on the speaker's physical position.
stops.uncertainty: The rocky rise is a schematic reminder of one possible meaning. It is not evidence that the address occurred outdoors on that hill.

perspectives.paul: What questions are put to Paul in verses 19–20? Separate those recorded questions from any motives you might imagine.
perspectives.listener: What do the listeners say they want to understand? What information is absent about the meeting's procedure?
perspectives.archaeologist: How does a name that can denote a hill or a council limit a reconstructed scene?

stops.title: An address and varied responses
stops.textNote: Read the address as transmitted in Acts, followed by the distinct responses in verses 32–34. The perspective prompts ask about this text; they add no character dialogue.
stops.evidenceNote: The Greek Ministry's conservation account describes restored routes, conserved architectural remains and modern visitor facilities around the Agora and Areopagus. Today's visitor landscape therefore needs interpretation too.
stops.uncertainty: No altar model, audience portrait or speech location is claimed here. Material remains and a narrated speech answer different historical questions.

perspectives.paul: Which observations and quotations form the address in verses 22–31? Follow the sequence without supplying extra words.
perspectives.listener: List the responses that verses 32–34 actually name. Which listeners are named, and which remain anonymous?
perspectives.archaeologist: What can an excavated or restored place contribute to reading this episode, and what can it leave unresolved?
